references.citation: Schreier, O. (1926). "Über die Erweiterung von Gruppen I." Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik 34: 165–180; Schreier, O. (1926). "Über die Erweiterung von Gruppen II." Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 4: 321–346.
references.relevance: Schreier's two 1926 papers introduce the systematic theory of **group extensions** that powers the embedding-problem reformulation in keyInsight #6. For a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$ with quotient $Q = G/N$, Schreier showed that extensions $1 \to N \to G \to Q \to 1$ are classified by *factor systems* — set-theoretic 2-cocycles $f: Q \times Q \to N$ satisfying an associativity condition modulo coboundaries. This is the historical seed of the cohomological reformulation by Eilenberg-MacLane (next entry), and the structural mechanism by which Shafarevich's inductive proof lifts a Galois realization of $G/N$ to one of $G$: each step reduces to choosing a factor system that is *cohomologous to zero* in $H^2(Q, N)$, the existence of which is verified by class field theory + Tate-Poitou duality. Cited in keyInsight #6 as the structural backbone of the embedding-problem framework.

references.citation: Eilenberg, S., MacLane, S. (1947). "Cohomology Theory in Abstract Groups, II." Annals of Mathematics, Second Series, 48(2): 326–341.
references.relevance: The paper establishing the **cohomological classification of group extensions**: the second cohomology group $H^2(Q, N)$ of $Q$ with coefficients in $N$ (with the induced $Q$-action) is in natural bijection with isomorphism classes of extensions $1 \to N \to G \to Q \to 1$. This converts Schreier's factor-system calculus into a *functorial cohomological obstruction theory* — exactly what keyInsight #6 invokes when it states that the embedding problem reduces to verifying that an obstruction class in $H^2(\mathrm{Gal}, N)$ vanishes via the local-global principle and class field theory. Combined with Schreier 1926, Eilenberg-MacLane 1947 is the algebraic foundation on which Shafarevich's inductive proof structure rests: at each step, the obstruction lives in $H^2$, and class field theory + Brauer-group machinery discharge it for abelian $N$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Cited in keyInsight #6.

references.citation: Demushkin, S. P. (1959). "The group of a maximal $p$-extension of a local field." Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat. 23: 329–346.
references.relevance: Demushkin's paper — written under Shafarevich's supervision — provides the **fix to the prime-2 gap in Shafarevich's 1954 proof** cited in keyInsight #9. Shafarevich's original argument used a local 2-adic computation in cyclotomic units that contained an error specific to $p = 2$; Demushkin (1959) introduced what are now called *Demushkin groups* — the pro-$p$ Galois groups of maximal $p$-extensions of local fields — and computed their structure correctly for $p = 2$. The corrected version, sometimes called the **Shafarevich-Demushkin theorem**, is what is now the canonical reference (and what modern accounts in Neukirch-Schmidt-Wingberg, already referenced, present). Demushkin's theory of pro-$p$ groups is also the foundational input to Iwasawa theory's $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extensions, completing the connection to openQuestion #3 on Shafarevich-Iwasawa formulations.

references.citation: Iwasawa, K. (1953). "On Galois groups of local fields." Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 80: 448–469; Iwasawa, K. (1973). "On $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$-extensions of algebraic number fields." Annals of Mathematics, Second Series, 98(2): 246–326.
references.relevance: Iwasawa's foundational papers on Galois groups of local fields (1953) and the structure theory of $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extensions (1973) — the substrate of *Iwasawa theory* that underlies the **Shafarevich-Iwasawa conjecture** stated in openQuestion #3. Iwasawa's 1973 paper introduces the characteristic ideal of an Iwasawa module and the Main Conjecture (proved by Mazur-Wiles 1984 for totally real fields), giving the cohomological framework in which absolute Galois groups of number fields acquire computable arithmetic invariants. The Shafarevich-Iwasawa conjecture combines Shafarevich's solvable realizability with Iwasawa's structural-group description of $G_{\mathbb{Q}, S}$ (absolute Galois group of the maximal extension unramified outside $S$) to predict that $G_{\mathbb{Q}, S}$ is a *projective profinite group* with a specific finite presentation. Cited in openQuestion #3.

references.citation: Harbater, D. (1994). "Galois coverings of the arithmetic line." In *Number Theory: New York 1984–1985*, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1240, Springer, pp. 165–195; and Harbater, D. (1995). "Fundamental groups and embedding problems in characteristic p." Contemp. Math. 186, pp. 353–369.
references.relevance: Harbater's 1994/1995 work on the **geometric (function-field) inverse Galois problem** — referenced explicitly in openQuestion #7 of this file ("Geometric Shafarevich (Harbater 1994, Pop 1995)"). Harbater proves that every finite group $G$ is realizable as the Galois group of a Galois cover of the projective line $\mathbb{P}^1_{\overline{k}}$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ of arbitrary characteristic, by patching local-to-global formal-scheme constructions. This is a **complete solution** of the inverse Galois problem in the geometric (function-field) setting — sharpening exactly what Shafarevich's 1954 theorem (this file's central axiom) leaves open over $\mathbb{Q}$: where the number-field problem remains open for general non-solvable groups, the function-field problem is fully solved. The contrast is foundational for openQuestion #7: it pinpoints precisely which features of the number-field setting (e.g., the lack of "enough" $\mathbb{Q}$-rational points on parameterizing varieties, the absence of a Riemann existence theorem analogue, the arithmetic delicacy of descent from $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ to $\mathbb{Q}$) obstruct an analogous proof over $\mathbb{Q}$.

references.citation: Pop, F. (1995). "Étale Galois covers of affine smooth curves." Inventiones Mathematicae 120(3): 555–578; and Pop, F. (1996). "Embedding problems over large fields." Annals of Mathematics 144(1): 1–34.
references.relevance: Pop's 1995/1996 papers — referenced in openQuestion #7 alongside Harbater 1994 — give an **independent, complementary proof** of the function-field inverse Galois problem: every finite group is realizable as $\mathrm{Gal}(L/k(t))$ over a function field $k(t)$ for $k$ algebraically closed (1995, via étale Galois covers of affine smooth curves), and more generally embedding problems over **large fields** (e.g., pseudo-algebraically-closed fields, real-closed fields, $p$-adically-closed fields) are solvable for every finite split embedding problem (1996, the foundational paper on large fields and the inverse Galois problem). Pop's *large-field criterion* — that a field $K$ is large if every smooth $K$-curve with a $K$-rational point has infinitely many — provides the abstract structural condition under which the function-field inverse Galois result lifts: Shafarevich's 1954 theorem over $\mathbb{Q}$ corresponds to the (still open) question of whether $\mathbb{Q}$ is, or can be replaced by, a large field for the purposes of solvable embedding problems. Together with Harbater's patching approach, Pop's work establishes that the function-field inverse Galois problem is complete; the obstruction to extending to $\mathbb{Q}$ is precisely the failure of $\mathbb{Q}$ to be large.

references.citation: Belyi, G. V. (1979). "On Galois extensions of a maximal cyclotomic field." Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR, Ser. Mat. 43(2): 269–276; English translation in Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya 14(2) (1980): 247–256.
references.relevance: Belyi's three-point theorem — **the crucial input** for the historicalContext claim that Matzat (1985), Thompson (1984), and others realized all finite simple groups of Lie type over $\mathbb{Q}$ via rigidity and Belyi's theorem. The theorem states that a smooth projective curve $X / \mathbb{C}$ is defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ if and only if $X$ admits a non-constant morphism $\beta : X \to \mathbb{P}^1$ ramified only over $\{0, 1, \infty\}$ (a *Belyi map*). For the non-solvable inverse Galois program post-Shafarevich, Belyi's theorem provides the bridge from rigid triples $(g_0, g_1, g_\infty) \in G^3$ with $g_0 g_1 g_\infty = 1$ generating $G$ — pure group-theoretic data — to Galois covers of $\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0, 1, \infty\}$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, which then descend to $\mathbb{Q}$ when the rigid triple is *rational* (closed under $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ action). This is the engine of every non-solvable realization in the historicalContext list: $S_n / A_n$ via $x^n - x - 1$ (Hilbert 1892), Lie-type groups via rigidity (Matzat 1985, Thompson 1984), and 25 of 26 sporadic simple groups including the Monster (Borcherds 1989–1992).

references.citation: Matzat, B. H. (1987). *Konstruktive Galoistheorie.* Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1284, Springer.
references.relevance: Matzat's monograph — referenced in historicalContext for the post-Shafarevich progress on non-solvable simple groups of Lie type — develops the **rigidity criterion** for the inverse Galois problem: a finite group $G$ is rigid over $\mathbb{Q}$ if it admits a $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$-stable rigid triple of generators, and rigidity implies realizability over $\mathbb{Q}$ via Belyi-theorem-based descent. Matzat used rigidity to realize many classical Lie-type simple groups (e.g., $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ for many $p$, the Suzuki groups, the Mathieu groups $M_{11}, M_{12}, M_{22}, M_{24}$) over $\mathbb{Q}$. The book is the canonical reference for the *constructive* (Belyi-rigid-triple-based) approach to non-solvable inverse Galois — the direct sibling of the *axiomatic/cohomological* approach this file takes for the solvable case via Shafarevich's theorem.

references.citation: Borcherds, R. E. (1992). "Monstrous moonshine and monstrous Lie superalgebras." Inventiones Mathematicae 109(1): 405–444.
references.relevance: Borcherds's 1992 proof of the **monstrous moonshine conjecture** — referenced in historicalContext as the key input for the realization of the Monster group $\mathbb{M}$ as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ (one of the 25 of 26 sporadic simple groups realized as of 2026). Borcherds constructs the Monster as the automorphism group of the moonshine vertex operator algebra $V^\natural$ (Frenkel-Lepowsky-Meurman 1988), and exploits the modular-form structure of the McKay-Thompson series $T_g(\tau) = \sum_n \mathrm{tr}(g | V^\natural_n) q^n$ for $g \in \mathbb{M}$. The Galois-realization input is that the modular curve $X_0(N)$ for appropriate $N$ admits a Monster-equivariant cover, which (via Belyi's theorem and Matzat's rigidity machinery) descends to a $\mathbb{Q}$-rational Galois extension realizing $\mathbb{M}$. The result places the Monster — the largest sporadic simple group, order $\approx 8 \times 10^{53}$ — within the realized portion of the post-Shafarevich non-solvable inverse Galois landscape, leaving only $M_{23}$ as the lone unrealized sporadic (referenced in openQuestion #6 and the cross-reference to `inverse-galois-oq-02`).

references.citation: Burnside, W. (1904). "On groups of order $p^\alpha q^\beta$." Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, Second Series, 1: 388–392.
references.relevance: Burnside's 1904 theorem — every finite group of order $p^a q^b$ is solvable — is the **computable order test** that widens Shafarevich's reach to a finite computation, as detailed in keyInsight #8. For any group $G$ whose order has at most two distinct prime factors, $G$ is solvable (Burnside) and therefore Galois-realizable over $\mathbb{Q}$ (Shafarevich, this file's axiom). The threshold is sharp at $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ (three distinct primes), and $A_5$ is the smallest non-solvable group. This combination — Burnside's solvability criterion + Shafarevich's realizability axiom — provides the gallery's gating tool: *every finite group of order $\leq 59$ is automatically Shafarevich-realizable*, as cataloged in the cross-reference to `abel-ruffini-galois-extensions-oq-07` (Burnside formalization). Cited in keyInsight #8.
